facts.claim: "Canola Fields" is the opening track of James McMurtry's album The Horses and the Hounds, released August 20, 2021 on New West Records.
McMurtry is the sole credited writer of "Canola Fields".
The album, including this song, was produced by Ross Hogarth, who also recorded and mixed it. Hogarth had recorded McMurtry's first two albums.

The album was recorded mainly at Jackson Browne's Groovemasters in Santa Monica, with more recording at Infinitespin Records in Van Nuys and Arlyn Studios in Austin. Additional recording was done at The Zone in Dripping Springs, Texas.
McMurtry said the band tracked the album in June 2019. The pandemic delayed the overdubs and mixing, and the release timing was the label's decision.
The song was released June 9, 2021 as the lead single when the album was announced. It was the first McMurtry album in about seven years, following 2015's Complicated Game.
McMurtry said the song formed over time. It grew from the fields he saw in Alberta and a roadside sign reading 'Canola Processing' with a phone number.

The song opens with the narrator thinking of someone while crossing Southern Alberta canola fields, and the fields' color recalls a chartreuse '69 Bug once driven around San Jose. The lyrics also mention Santa Cruz and Los Gatos.
McMurtry said "Canola Fields" and "Jackie" were his favorite songs on the album.
"Canola Fields" was nominated for Song of the Year at the 2022 Americana Music Honors & Awards. Brandi Carlile's "Right on Time" won.
McMurtry is the son of novelist Larry McMurtry. John Mellencamp co-produced his 1989 debut Too Long in the Wasteland, and the 2006 Americana Song of the Year went to his "We Can't Make It Here".

research.lineage: The song sits in the Austin-based Americana, roots-rock and alt-country singer-songwriter tradition, with literate story-songs and character sketches.

draft:
A field of canola in Southern Alberta turns the exact yellow-green of a '69 Volkswagen Beetle, and suddenly James McMurtry's narrator is back in San Jose, decades younger, watching someone he loved drive it around town. That's how **Canola Fields** opens, and it's a perfect picture of how memory actually works: not a decision to look back, but a color that ambushes you from the highway. McMurtry has said the song grew slowly out of those Alberta fields and a roadside sign advertising canola processing, phone number and all. It's the kind of mundane detail a good storyteller hoards until it earns a place.

What follows is a whole friendship told in road trips. There's an old white Lincoln with suicide doors and always room for more, then a bad ride back from Santa Cruz watching a surfer win her over. The narrator admits more than he means to: "And I coulda cut his throat." He blames the whiskey, insists they were never really a couple, then shuts the door twice: he doesn't want to think about that. The jealousy, the shame, and the self-defense all stay in the room together, unresolved, which is exactly how old regret feels.

The second half brings them back together years later, in Brooklyn, where she's living with her sister and walking with her keys clenched in her fist. That small, guarded detail does a lot of work. Life hasn't been easy on either of them. On a cross-town bus they finally act on a crush thirty years old, and McMurtry lands the line of the song: "You can't be young and do that." It's half rueful, half grateful. Youth would have wrecked it. The repetitions pile up as the song goes on, and the line starts to sound like something he's still convincing himself of. The chorus is a plain, scared plea to Marie: "Take a death grip on some part of me," before he drifts out to sea.

The band, cut in June 2019 with Ross Hogarth producing, keeps out of the way. Fingerpicked acoustic guitar, a bass walking the root notes, drums holding a steady mid-tempo shuffle. The room is dry and close. McMurtry's voice is gravelly and conversational, no harmonies, like a man telling you this across a kitchen table. It's squarely in the Austin story-song tradition, literate and unhurried, and it opened his first album in about seven years. McMurtry named it one of his two favorites on the record, and it earned an Americana Song of the Year nomination.

What sticks is how the song lets loneliness and gratitude share one breath: you hear a man admit he's adrift, and still treasure the late, unlikely moment someone held on.

factCheck.note: Matches the researched facts: the song formed over time from the fields and a 'Canola Processing' sign with a phone number.
